slides.title: Article 19 TEU
slides.text: Two sentences that do very different jobs. First: the Court of Justice of the European Union SHALL INCLUDE the Court of Justice, the General Court and specialised courts, and shall ensure that in the interpretation and application of the Treaties the law is observed. Second: MEMBER STATES shall provide remedies sufficient to ensure effective legal protection in the fields covered by Union law. The second sentence is the one that became the constitutional weapon in the rule-of-law cases — judicial independence in the member states is an EU law requirement because of it.

cards.q: What obligation does Article 19(1) second subparagraph TEU place on member states?
cards.a: To provide remedies sufficient to ensure effective legal protection in the fields covered by Union law — the basis on which the Court reviews national judicial independence.

slides.title: The structure of the CJEU
slides.text: 'Court of Justice of the European Union' is the umbrella term. Under it sit the Court of Justice (the ECJ), the General Court, and possible specialised tribunals under Article 257 TFEU. Calling the whole institution 'the ECJ' is a common slip.

cards.q: What does 'Court of Justice of the European Union' cover?
cards.a: The institution as a whole: the Court of Justice (ECJ), the General Court, and any specialised courts under Article 257 TFEU.

slides.title: Composition and formations
slides.text: The Court of Justice: 27 judges, one per member state, plus 11 Advocates General. The General Court: 54 judges, two per member state. Formations: chambers of three, chambers of five, the Grand Chamber of 15 judges, and the full Court. The Advocate General is the feature with no national equivalent — an impartial member of the Court who delivers a reasoned opinion before judgment, which does not bind but is often followed.

terms.def: A member of the Court delivering an independent reasoned opinion on the case before judgment; not binding.

cards.q: How many judges sit in the Court of Justice and in the General Court, and what is the Grand Chamber?
cards.a: 27 judges (one per member state) plus 11 Advocates General in the Court of Justice; 54 judges (two per member state) in the General Court. The Grand Chamber is a formation of 15 judges.

slides.title: Appointment of judges
slides.text: Under Article 255 TFEU a panel gives an opinion on candidates' suitability before the member states appoint them by common accord.

slides.title: The Article 255 panel itself
slides.text: The photographs are the current members of the panel — the 'comité' — and the fact worth taking from the slide is its composition. Under ARTICLE 255(2) TFEU the panel comprises SEVEN PERSONS chosen from among FORMER MEMBERS of the Court of Justice and the General Court, MEMBERS OF NATIONAL SUPREME COURTS and LAWYERS OF RECOGNISED COMPETENCE, ONE of whom is PROPOSED BY THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT. The Council appoints them on the initiative of the President of the Court of Justice. The panel gives a non-binding opinion on a candidate's suitability, but in practice a negative opinion ends the candidacy, which is why a body invented only in Lisbon has quietly become the real filter on who sits in Luxembourg.

cards.q: How is the Article 255 TFEU panel composed?
cards.a: SEVEN persons, chosen from FORMER MEMBERS of the Court of Justice and the General Court, MEMBERS OF NATIONAL SUPREME COURTS and LAWYERS OF RECOGNISED COMPETENCE — ONE of them PROPOSED BY THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT. The Council appoints them on the initiative of the President of the Court of Justice.

cards.q: Is the Article 255 panel's opinion binding on the member states?
cards.a: Formally NO — it is an opinion on the candidate's suitability, and the judges are still appointed by COMMON ACCORD of the governments. In practice a negative opinion ends the candidacy, so the panel has become the real filter on appointments.

slides.title: The four main procedures
slides.text: Preliminary reference, Article 267 TFEU. Infringement, Articles 258-260 TFEU. Action for annulment, Articles 263 and 264 TFEU. Action for failure to act, Article 265 TFEU. If an exam question asks how a particular grievance reaches the Court, the answer is almost always one of these four — and choosing the right one is half the marks.

cards.q: Name the four main procedures before the CJEU with their Treaty articles.
cards.a: Preliminary reference (Art 267 TFEU), infringement (Arts 258-260), action for annulment (Arts 263-264), and action for failure to act (Art 265).

slides.title: The other procedures
slides.text: Damages against the Union (Art 268), actions on arbitration clauses in Union contracts (Art 272) and between member states (Art 273), staff cases (Art 270 with 256(1), 257), opinions on the compatibility of intended international agreements (Art 218(11)), sanction proceedings under Article 7 TEU (Art 269), and miscellaneous matters (Art 271).

slides.title: Who hears what
slides.text: The division of jurisdiction under Article 256 TFEU and Article 51 of the Statute. The COURT OF JUSTICE takes preliminary rulings (Art 267), infringement proceedings (Arts 258, 259) and opinions on international agreements (Art 218(11)). The GENERAL COURT takes actions for annulment (Art 263), failure to act (Art 265) and damages (Art 268) — the direct actions typically brought by individuals and companies — with appeals on points of law going up to the Court of Justice.

cards.q: A company wants to annul a Commission decision addressed to it. Which court, and what happens on appeal?
cards.a: The General Court, which hears actions for annulment, failure to act and damages. An appeal on points of law lies to the Court of Justice.

slides.title: Caseload statistics
slides.text: A chart from the Court's Annual Report showing how large a share of its work preliminary references are.

slides.title: Jurisdiction over references
slides.text: Exclusively the Court of Justice under Article 267(1) TFEU, with the possibility of transferring defined areas to the General Court under Article 256(3) TFEU — a possibility that has recently begun to be used.

slides.title: The four questions
slides.text: The structure for any reference problem: is the referring body a COURT OR TRIBUNAL of a member state; is the SUBJECT MATTER within Article 267; is the question RELEVANT; and is there a right or a duty to refer?

slides.title: What counts as a court or tribunal
slides.text: The Vaassen criteria (Case 61/65), and they are a checklist: the body must be established BY LAW, be PERMANENT, be INDEPENDENT, have MANDATORY jurisdiction, apply an ADVERSARIAL procedure, and be obliged to apply RULES OF LAW. Note that 'court or tribunal' is an autonomous EU law concept — what the national system calls the body does not decide.

terms.def: Established by law, permanent, independent, compulsory jurisdiction, inter partes procedure, applying rules of law.

cards.q: List the Vaassen criteria for a 'court or tribunal of a Member State' under Article 267 TFEU.
cards.a: Established by law; permanent; independent; with compulsory jurisdiction; applying an adversarial procedure; and bound to apply rules of law. The concept is autonomous EU law, not national labels.

slides.title: Who is excluded
slides.text: The Court applies the criteria strictly and non-functionally. No reference from an ADMINISTRATIVE AUTHORITY entrusted with deciding appeals against administrative decisions — Corbiau (C-24/92), Anesco (C-462/19), because it is not independent of the administration whose decision it reviews. And no reference from an ARBITRAL TRIBUNAL — Nordsee (102/81), because its jurisdiction rests on the parties' agreement rather than being compulsory.

cards.q: Can an arbitral tribunal make a preliminary reference?
cards.a: No — Nordsee (102/81): its jurisdiction derives from the parties' agreement, not from law, so it lacks compulsory jurisdiction. Nor can an administrative authority deciding appeals against the administration (Corbiau, Anesco).

slides.title: Two subject matters
slides.text: Article 267(1) allows two kinds of question. INTERPRETATION of the Treaties and of other EU acts, including secondary law. And VALIDITY of EU acts, which turns on their compatibility with higher EU law. The distinction matters for who may refer, as the next slides show.

slides.title: Relevance
slides.text: Article 267(2): EU law must be applicable to the case in the main proceedings, and the question must be NECESSARY to enable the national court to give judgment. And the warning in bold: no question on the interpretation of NATIONAL law — the Court answers about EU law and leaves the national provision to the referring court.

cards.q: A national court asks the CJEU whether its own statute is compatible with a directive. Is the question admissible as framed?
cards.a: Not as framed: the Court does not interpret national law or rule on its compatibility. The question must be reformulated to ask how the EU provision is to be interpreted, leaving the application to the referring court.

slides.title: Right and duty to refer
slides.text: The matrix to memorise. INTERPRETATION: any court or tribunal MAY refer (Art 267(2)); a court against whose decisions there is no judicial remedy under national law MUST refer (Art 267(3)). VALIDITY: any court or tribunal may refer — and must, if it thinks the act invalid, because Foto-Frost (314/85) reserves to the Court of Justice alone the power to declare an EU act invalid. A national court may uphold validity; it may never strike an EU act down itself.

terms.def: Only the Court of Justice may declare an EU act invalid; national courts must refer if they consider an act invalid.

cards.q: A first-instance national court is convinced an EU regulation is invalid. What must it do?
cards.a: Refer to the Court of Justice. Under Foto-Frost (314/85) only the CJEU may declare an EU act invalid; a national court may uphold validity but never set the act aside itself — and this applies at any instance.

cards.q: Which courts are obliged to refer a question of interpretation?
cards.a: Courts or tribunals against whose decisions there is no judicial remedy under national law — Article 267(3) TFEU.

slides.title: The right to refer is the court's alone
slides.text: Three propositions with teeth. The decision to refer is the SOLE DISCRETION of the national court. Miasto Łowicz (C-558/18 and C-563/18): no disciplinary proceedings may be brought against judges for referring. Cartesio (C-210/06): it is incompatible with EU law for appeal courts to amend or set aside the question referred. And from the parties' side: they may propose a reference, but the court is under no obligation to follow the request.

cards.q: Can a higher national court quash or rewrite a lower court's reference to the CJEU?
cards.a: No — Cartesio (C-210/06). And under Miasto Łowicz a judge may not be disciplined for referring. The decision to refer belongs to the referring court alone.

slides.title: CILFIT: when a last-instance court need not refer
slides.text: Case 283/81 carves three exceptions out of the duty in Article 267(3). ACTE ÉCLAIRÉ I: the same legal question has already been answered in a similar case. ACTE ÉCLAIRÉ II: the question is not identical but so similar to answered case law that the answer is clear from it. ACTE CLAIR: there is no case law, but the correct interpretation is so utterly obvious that there is no room for reasonable doubt — for that court, for the Court of Justice, and for any other court in the EU. The last condition is deliberately near-impossible, which is why acte clair is pleaded far more often than it succeeds.

terms.def: The correct interpretation is so obvious as to leave no scope for reasonable doubt in any court of the Union.
The question has already been answered by the Court's case law.

cards.q: When is a last-instance court relieved of the duty to refer under CILFIT?
cards.a: Where the same question has already been answered (acte éclairé I); where existing case law makes the answer clear even if the question is not identical (acte éclairé II); or where the correct interpretation is so obvious as to leave no reasonable doubt for any court in the Union (acte clair).

slides.title: What follows from breaching the duty
slides.text: Three layers of consequence. EU LAW: state liability for a violation by a national court — Köbler (C-224/01) — and an infringement action against the member state for failing to comply with Article 267(3), as in Commission v France (C-416/17). NATIONAL LAW: in Austria there is no individual party right to a referral (OGH 1 Ob 354/97h), but a failure to refer violates the right to the lawful judge under Article 83(2) B-VG. And the ECHR: Article 6(1) — an arbitrary refusal to refer can breach the right to a fair trial.

cards.q: A last-instance court refuses to refer without reasons. What remedies does the losing party have?
cards.a: Under EU law, a Köbler claim for state liability, and the Commission may bring an infringement action (Commission v France C-416/17). In Austria, a breach of the right to the lawful judge under Art 83(2) B-VG. Under the ECHR, a possible violation of Article 6(1).

slides.title: The effect of the judgment
slides.text: Three properties. It is a BINDING ruling on EU law for the referring court. It has ERGA OMNES effect, so other courts and authorities must follow it and member states are obliged to change conflicting provisions. And it takes effect EX TUNC — from the beginning — unless the Court expressly limits its temporal effects, which it does mainly in invalidity cases to protect legal certainty.

cards.q: What is the effect of a preliminary ruling in time and as to persons?
cards.a: It binds the referring court, has erga omnes effect on all other courts and authorities, and applies ex tunc — unless the Court expressly limits its temporal effects.

slides.title: A worked example: Google v CNIL
slides.text: The remaining slides follow case C-507/17 through the procedure from reference to judgment.

slides.title: How a reference starts
slides.text: The questions, drafted by the court and often suggested by the lawyers, go to the Registrar; the national court must STAY its proceedings until the CJEU rules (Art 23 Statute). In this case the referring court was the French Conseil d'État, by decision of 19 July 2017.

slides.title: The Registrar's role
slides.text: The Registrar notifies the claimant, the defendant, the member states and the national court under Article 23 of the Statute.

slides.title: The Judge-Rapporteur
slides.text: The President of the Court — Koen Lenaerts at the time — designates a Judge-Rapporteur under Article 15 of the Rules of Procedure; here Marko Ilešič.

slides.title: The Advocate General
slides.text: The First Advocate General designates the Advocate General under Article 16 of the Rules of Procedure; here Maciej Szpunar.

slides.title: The written procedure
slides.text: Under Article 23 of the Statute participants have TWO MONTHS to submit observations; member states may use their own language, others must use the language of the case, and observations are translated into the language of the case and into French — which remains the Court's main working language. Under Article 40 other member states and third parties may intervene: member states and EU institutions without restriction, others only with legal personality and a specific interest.

cards.q: Who may submit observations in a preliminary reference procedure?
cards.a: The parties, the member states and the Commission under Article 23 of the Statute, within two months. Other member states and EU institutions may intervene without restriction; other parties need legal personality and a specific interest (Art 40 Statute).

slides.title: Article 23 notification applied: Google v CNIL
slides.text: The same Registrar diagram, now filled in with the actual reference. The CONSEIL D'ÉTAT — the French national court — sends the questions to the Court, and from that moment everything runs through the REGISTRAR, who notifies, under ARTICLE 23 OF THE STATUTE, the parties to the main proceedings (here GOOGLE as claimant and the CNIL, the French data protection authority, as defendant), the MEMBER STATE whose court made the reference, the other member states, and the COMMISSION. Each of them then has TWO MONTHS to send written observations. The case is C-507/17, Google v CNIL — the right-to-be-forgotten reference about whether de-referencing must be worldwide. What the diagram is teaching is not the substance of that case but the shape of the procedure: a preliminary reference is NOT a private dispute that happens to reach Luxembourg. The national court is the only one who asks; the parties, every member state and the Commission are all merely invited to comment, and they comment to the COURT, not to each other.

cards.q: In Google v CNIL (C-507/17), who was notified of the reference under Article 23 of the Statute?
cards.a: The Registrar notified the PARTIES to the main proceedings (Google as claimant, the CNIL as defendant), the MEMBER STATE whose court referred (France, through the Conseil d'État) and the other member states, and the COMMISSION. Each then had TWO MONTHS to submit written observations.

cards.q: Who actually puts the questions to the Court in a preliminary reference, and what is everyone else's role?
cards.a: Only the NATIONAL COURT asks. The parties, the member states and the Commission are merely NOTIFIED by the Registrar under Article 23 of the Statute and invited to submit observations TO THE COURT within two months — a preliminary reference is a dialogue between courts, not a private dispute that travelled to Luxembourg.

slides.title: The interveners
slides.text: In Google v CNIL the interveners included the Wikimedia Foundation, the Fondation pour la liberté de la presse, Microsoft, the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, Article 19, the Internet Freedom Foundation and the Défenseur des droits — an illustration of how a reference becomes a public interest litigation.

slides.title: End of the written stage
slides.text: The Judge-Rapporteur produces a preliminary report (Art 59 Rules of Procedure) for the general meeting, which decides whether clarifications are needed from the referring court, in which formation the case is heard — here the Grand Chamber — whether to dispense with a hearing, and whether to dispense with the Advocate General's Opinion, which is possible only where the case raises no new point of law (Art 20 Statute).

slides.title: When there is no oral hearing
slides.text: A hearing is held on reasoned request by an Article 23 entity. There is none if the case is manifestly inadmissible (Art 53(2) RoP); if the Judge-Rapporteur and Advocate General consider there is already sufficient information (Art 76(2)); or if the question is identical to one already answered and the answer is clear (Art 99).

slides.title: The hearing
slides.text: Directed by the President; the Advocate General and the judges may ask questions; public except where held in camera for security or the protection of minors. In this case the hearing was on 11 September 2018 and the Advocate General's opinion followed on 10 January 2019.

slides.title: The judgment
slides.text: Either a reasoned order (Arts 53(2), 99 RoP) or a judgment. The structure is always the same and is worth knowing when reading cases: participants; legal context, EU and national; the national dispute; the questions referred; consideration of the questions, with the parties' arguments and the Court's decision; costs; and the OPERATIVE PART — the paragraph at the end that actually answers the question and is the part to quote.

cards.q: Which part of a CJEU judgment answers the referred question?
cards.a: The operative part at the end. The preceding sections set out the legal context, the dispute, the questions and the reasoning.

slides.title: Jurisdiction
slides.text: Exclusively the Court of Justice — Article 258 TFEU with Article 256 TFEU and Article 51 of the Statute.

slides.title: Who can bring it
slides.text: The Commission under Article 258, and — far more rarely — another member state under Article 259. Both are directed against the member state alleged to have violated EU law.

cards.q: Who may bring infringement proceedings against a member state?
cards.a: The Commission under Article 258 TFEU and another member state under Article 259 TFEU. In practice almost all cases are brought by the Commission.

slides.title: The Commission's procedure
slides.text: Three stages. An INFORMAL phase of contacts. Then the PRE-LITIGATION procedure in two formal steps: a letter of formal notice, and then a reasoned opinion setting a deadline. Only if the state fails to comply does the Commission go to the Court. The pre-litigation stage is not a formality: it defines the subject-matter, and the Commission cannot later raise complaints in Court that were not in the reasoned opinion.

terms.term: letter of formal notice / reasoned opinion
terms.def: The two formal steps of the pre-litigation stage of an infringement procedure.

cards.q: Set out the stages of an infringement procedure brought by the Commission.
cards.a: Informal contacts; the pre-litigation procedure — letter of formal notice, then reasoned opinion with a deadline; and only then an application to the Court of Justice. The reasoned opinion fixes the subject-matter of the later action.

slides.title: The member state's procedure
slides.text: Under Article 259 the applicant member state must first involve the Commission: adversarial proceedings before it, after which the Commission delivers a reasoned opinion — or, if it does not, the member state may bring its own claim to the Court.

slides.title: Judgment and what follows
slides.text: Three stages again. STAGE 1, Article 260(1): a declaration of infringement with erga omnes effect; the member state is obliged to take all measures necessary to comply. STAGE 2, Article 260(2): if it does not, the Commission opens a second procedure, giving the state a deadline and then applying to the Court, proposing a lump sum or penalty payment. STAGE 3: the Court may impose that lump sum or penalty, with discretion as to the amount. And the shortcut in Article 260(3): for FAILURE TO TRANSPOSE a directive, the Commission may ask for a financial penalty already in the FIRST judgment — no second round needed.

terms.def: For failure to notify transposition measures for a directive, a financial penalty may be imposed in the first infringement judgment.

cards.q: A member state ignores an infringement judgment. What can the Commission do?
cards.a: Open a second procedure under Article 260(2): give the state a deadline, then apply to the Court proposing a lump sum and/or penalty payment, which the Court may impose in its discretion.

cards.q: What is special about Article 260(3) TFEU?
cards.a: Where the infringement is a failure to notify measures transposing a legislative directive, the Court may impose a lump sum or penalty payment already in the FIRST judgment, without a second set of proceedings.
